newsitem.title: UK: BADMINTON-CHINA IN NEAR CLEAN SWEEP.
newsitem.headline: BADMINTON-CHINA IN NEAR CLEAN SWEEP.

text.p: Tears shed on the rostrum in Atlanta were forgotten on Saturday as Dong Jiong, Olympic silver medallist, won the All England badminton men's singles final, brushing aside Chinese compatriot Sun Jun 15-9 15-5.
In the women's final, world champion Ye Zhaoying, also of China, layed another ghost to rest.

She overwhelmed compatriot Gong Zhichao 11-1 11-3 and helped erase memories of 12 months ago when she suffered a crushing 11-1 11-1 humiliation at the hands of now retired Bang Soo-hyun of South Korea.
China went on to take two of the other three titles on offer to record their best ever performance in the 87 years of the tournament.
Both men's finalists turned up for a news conference after their match but when an official, acting as an interpreter, realised a Malaysian television crew was present the Chinese left.
The reason given was that the players had to change out of their kit but it appeared their exit was due to political sensitivities. The players did not return.
Dong, probably the most explosive player on the men's circuit, had gained revenge late on Friday on Poul-Erik Hoyer-Larsen, who took the Olympic gold last summer.
He overcame the tall Dane in straight games, a perfect prelude for Saturday's win over Sun Jun, who claimed his final place with an excellent win over world champion Heryanto Arbi of Indonesia.
Truth to tell, however, the men's final was a lacklustre affair.
Dong was largely in control and the only time Sun, a former world junior champion, got within striking distance, he ruined his chance with errors near the net.
It was 23-year-old Dong's first major success and on current form the world championship in Glasgow in May looks well within his grasp.
The women's final produced an even duller display than the men's an hour earlier.
Gong, seeded two and at the age of 19 seen as the next big Chinese star, was a shadow of the player who had done so well earlier in the week.
She managed to save four match points at the end but it was all too little too late.
Later she struggled to explain the loss of form. "It's hard to say," she told reporters.
Ye, back to her best after a poor 1996, said: "This makes up for last year".
Twice runner-up here before winning on Saturday, she looked in good shape to retain her world crown in just over two months time.
It was China virtually all the way on Saturday, sounding a clear warning to the other power-houses of the sport, Indonesia, South Korea and Denmark.
Having monopolised both singles finals for the first time in the tournament's history, China also won the women's doubles and mixed doubles titles.
Top seeds Ge Fei and Gu Jun beat Eliza and Resiana Zelin of Indonesia 15-6 15-9, then Ge teamed up with Liu Yong to overcome top seeds Trikus Heryanto and Minarti Timur of Indonesia 15-10 15-2.

The only title not to go to the Chinese was the men's doubles. South Koreans Ha Tae-kwon and Kang Kyung-jin beat Denmark's Jon Holst-Christensen and Michael Sogaard 15-11 17-16 in by far the best match of the afternoon.
